levels.d: Start from yourself, talk to the living, and learn the records almost every family left behind.
Census pages, parish registers, passenger lists and wills: what each one really says, and what it leaves out.
Weigh evidence, cite as you go, resolve conflicts and plan your research instead of wandering.
Clusters, unindexed records, old handwriting and DNA: the techniques that open brick walls, and how to prove what you find.

lessons.title: Start with what you know
lessons.dek: Every family history is built backwards, one proven generation at a time, starting with you.

blocks.p: The most common beginner's mistake is to start with a famous name, a family legend or a distant ancestor and work forwards. It feels exciting, but it almost always ends with someone else's family attached to yours. Researchers who get it right do the opposite: they start with what they can **prove**, and step back one generation at a time.

blocks.h: Work from the known to the unknown

blocks.p: Begin with yourself: your birth, your parents' names, where and when they married. Then do the same for each parent, then each grandparent. Each new person should be connected to the last by a record that names them both: a birth certificate naming the parents, a marriage record naming the fathers, a census listing a child in a household.
It sounds slow. It is the fastest route in the end, because every step stands on the one before it.

Before you add a new generation, aim to find at least three records for the person you are standing on: something for their birth, their marriage and their death. Those three usually name the parents you need next.

The best records are often in a drawer. Families keep certificates, letters, funeral cards, photographs with names on the back, and bibles with births written inside the cover. Tick off what you can find, or ask relatives to look.

items: Birth, marriage and death certificates
Funeral cards, obituaries and newspaper cuttings
A family bible or prayer book with handwritten dates
Letters, postcards and diaries
Photographs, especially with writing on the back
Military papers, medals and service books
School reports, apprenticeship papers, union cards
Passports, naturalization papers, ship tickets
Address books and Christmas card lists

blocks.h: Write down where every fact came from

blocks.p: From day one, note where each fact came from: “Grandma, conversation, March 2026” or “Birth certificate, original in Mum's box.” It feels fussy until the day two sources disagree and you need to know which one to trust. In this app, add the record under **Records** on a person's profile and link it to the facts it supports.

quiz.q: You find a website tree claiming your great-grandfather descends from a medieval knight. What should you do first?
o: Add the knight and his line to your tree, then check it later
Keep researching back from yourself, and treat the claim as a lead to test
Ignore it: online trees are always wrong
quiz.why: Online trees are clues, not proof. Some are excellent, many copy each other's mistakes. Keep building back from what you can prove, and see whether your evidence eventually meets theirs.

takeaways: Start with yourself and step back one proven generation at a time.
Collect home sources before searching online.
Record where every fact came from, from the very first day.

lessons.title: Ask the living
lessons.dek: Your oldest relatives are an archive that closes. A good interview captures names, places and stories no record holds.

blocks.p: Records tell you *when* and *where*. People tell you *why*. Your relatives remember nicknames, the street a family lived on, which cousin emigrated and why nobody spoke to Uncle Frank. Those memories are often the clue that unlocks a record search years later.

Before you sit down, look at what you already know about the person's family, and bring a few photographs. Pictures are the best prompts there are: people remember far more when they have a face in front of them.

list: Ask permission to record, and record the whole conversation.
Start with their own life, not the distant past. People warm up talking about themselves.
Ask one question at a time, then wait. Silence is when the best stories come.
Ask for names and places to be spelled out.
Keep sessions short, under an hour, and come back.

blocks.p: A closed question gets a yes or a no. A leading question gets the answer you suggested. An open question gets a story, and stories are full of clues.

sort.prompt: Sort each question. Tap the type you think it is.
items: “What was a normal Sunday like when you were small?”
Open: it invites a description, with people, places and routines.
“Was your grandmother born in Ireland?”
Closed: it can be answered with one word. Try “Where did your grandmother grow up?”
“Your father fought at the Somme, didn't he?”
Leading: it plants the answer. They may agree to be polite.
“Tell me about the house you grew up in.”
Open: houses bring back neighbours, streets and who lived where.
“Did the family come over in 1912?”
Closed: try “How did the family come to live here?”
“I suppose they were very poor then?”
Leading: let them describe it in their own words.

blocks.p: Family stories shrink, stretch and travel. A grandfather who “came from Dublin” may have sailed from Dublin but been born in County Mayo. A famous relative is often a cousin, not a parent. Write the story down exactly as told, then test it against records. The kernel is usually true; the details drift.

blocks.t: The story about the name change
blocks.p: “Our name was changed at Ellis Island” is one of the most common family stories, and it is almost never true. Passenger lists were written at the port of departure, and US immigration officials didn't rename people. Changes usually happened later, by choice. Lesson 7 covers this.

quiz.q: Your aunt says her grandmother was “born in Galway in 1880.” What is the best way to record this?
o: Enter birth: 1880, Galway, and move on
Enter it, and note the source: “Aunt Joan, interview 2026, said ‘born in Galway in 1880’”
Don't enter it until you have a certificate
quiz.why: Capture it, with exactly who said it and when. It's a valuable lead, and recording its source tells your future self how much weight it can carry.

takeaways: Interview the oldest relatives first, and record it.
Use photographs as prompts, and ask open questions.
Treat every family story as a lead to test, and note who told it.

lessons.title: The core records
lessons.dek: Births, marriages, deaths, censuses and church registers will carry you most of the way back to 1800.

blocks.p: Thousands of record types exist, but three families of records do most of the work for most researchers. Knowing what each one contains, and when it starts, tells you where to look first.

Governments began registering births, marriages and deaths at different times. Before that date you will be relying on church records instead. Civil records are usually the most reliable for dates, and they name parents.

head: Place
Civil registration from
rows: By state, mostly 1880s–1920s; some towns much earlier

blocks.p: In England and Wales, the indexes are free on FreeBMD and the General Register Office site, and you order certificates from the GRO. Scotland's are on ScotlandsPeople, and Ireland's on IrishGenealogy.ie.

blocks.h: The census: households, every ten years

blocks.p: A census is a snapshot of a household on one night. It places a family in a street, lists the children (including ones who died young and left no other trace), and gives ages, birthplaces and occupations. Following a family census by census is the backbone of most research.

blocks.h: Church registers: before the state took over

blocks.p: Before civil registration, churches recorded baptisms, marriages and burials. They are the main source for the 1500s to the 1800s across Europe and the Americas. Note that a baptism is not a birth: it might be days, months or even years later.

sort.prompt: Which record would you reach for first? Tap one for each question.
items: Who were the parents of a woman married in Bolton in 1868?
Civil: an English marriage certificate from 1837 onwards names both fathers.
Which children lived with Thomas and Eliza in 1901?
Census: the 1901 census lists every person in the household that night.
When was a child baptised in Wigan in 1790?
Church: in England, there's no civil registration before July 1837.
What was James Ashworth's job in 1871?
Census: occupations are listed for each adult.
Exactly when did someone die in Ohio in 1938?
Civil: Ohio state death certificates began in December 1908.
Who were the godparents at a Hungarian christening in 1850?
Church: baptism registers name sponsors, and state registration didn't start in Hungary until 1895.

blocks.p: Most websites show an index first: a typed summary of a record. Indexes are wonderful for finding things, but they contain mistakes. Always look at the image of the original page when you can. It often holds more than the index does.

takeaways: Civil records, censuses and church registers do most of the work.
Know when civil registration starts in each place you research.
Use indexes to find records, and images to read them.
lib: CDC: Where to Write for Vital Records

lessons.title: Search like a researcher
lessons.dek: Names were spelled however the clerk heard them. Learn to search for the person, not the spelling.

blocks.p: Most of your ancestors could not read the forms that recorded them. The clerk wrote down what he heard, in the spelling he thought was right. One family can appear as Ashworth, Ashwith, Ashwort and Ashforth in the same decade. Searching only for the “correct” spelling means missing most of the records.

list: Search the surname alone, with a place and a date range, before adding a first name.
Give birth years a range of two to five years either side. Ages drift.
Try first names as initials, nicknames (Polly for Mary, Peggy for Margaret) and middle names.
Use wildcards where sites allow: Ash*th finds Ashworth and Ashwith.
Search for a parent, a sibling or a spouse instead. Find any one of them and you find the household.

blocks.p: Soundex is a code patented in 1918 and used in the 1930s to index the US census. It reduces a surname to its first letter and three digits for the consonant sounds that follow, so names that sound alike share a code. Many sites still use it, and it's a handy way to think up spellings you'd never have guessed.
Women usually appear under their father's surname before marriage and their husband's after, and sometimes under a second husband's later. When you lose a woman between censuses, look for a marriage.

Not everything is indexed, and indexes have gaps. If you know the parish and the year, browse the page images directly, a page at a time. It's slower, and it's how many brick walls fall. FamilySearch has millions of unindexed images reachable only through its catalog (Lesson 14).

quiz.q: You can't find Ann Crook, born about 1848, in the 1851 census. Which search is most likely to succeed?
o: Ann Crook, born 1848 exactly, Wigan
Surname Cr*k, born 1845–1851, Lancashire, with no first name
Ann Crook, born 1848, anywhere in the world
quiz.why: A wildcard surname catches Crook as well as misreadings like Crock or Cruck. A date range absorbs age errors. Dropping the first name finds the household even if she's listed as Hannah or Nancy.

takeaways: Search for the household, not just the person.
Use date ranges, wildcards and variant spellings.
When indexes fail, browse the images.

lessons.title: Reading a census
lessons.dek: One line of a census page holds half a dozen clues. Learn to read every column, and to distrust the ages.

blocks.p: Every census asks slightly different questions, but they share a shape: an address, then one line per person. Each column is a separate clue, and some are much more reliable than others.
Here is an invented entry for the example family, laid out like a page from the 1881 census of England. Tap any underlined cell to see what it tells you.

census.cap: Example record · 1881 census · 14 Back Cotton Street, Bolton, Lancashire
rows: Each line is one person present on census night, 3 April 1881. Someone working away, at sea or in hospital will be listed wherever they were.
The head of household. Every other relation is relative to him or her.
Ages are only as good as the person answering. Expect drift of a year or two between censuses, sometimes more.
Occupations point to other records: trade union books, factory records, apprenticeship papers.
Birthplace is a strong clue, but people sometimes gave the nearest town, or the place they grew up rather than where they were born.
Listed under her married name. Her maiden name, Holt, appears on the marriage record and her children's birth certificates.
Relationships to the head were first recorded in England in 1851, and in the US in 1880.
Compare ages across censuses. A woman who ages only eight years in a decade is common: wives were often recorded younger.
A blank doesn't mean she didn't work. Women's paid work, especially at home, was often left out.
Children are listed oldest first, usually. A gap of several years between children may hide one who died.
Thomas, born 1868, should be 12 or 13 here. This one fits.
‘Scholar’ means at school. In mill towns, children of this age might also be ‘half-timers’, splitting the day between school and the mill.
A widowed grandmother living with the family is a gift: she links this household to the generation before.
Mother of the head, so James's mother. This places Hannah, born about 1814, in the tree.
Widowed: her husband John died before 1881. Search for his death between the last census he appears in and this one.
Living on a small income or pension.
Born in Bury, not Bolton. Her baptism and marriage may be there.

blocks.p: People didn't always know their exact age, and whoever answered the door gave the information for everyone. In the 1841 census of England and Wales, enumerators were told to round the ages of anyone over 15 down to the nearest five, so a 38-year-old appears as 35.

quiz.q: Mary Ashworth is 29 in 1871, 39 in 1881 and 47 in 1891. What's the most reasonable conclusion?
o: These are probably three different Marys
Normal drift: she was born about 1842, and the 1891 age is a little off
The 1891 census is the most recent, so it must be right
quiz.why: Ages that are consistent in two censuses and off by a few years in a third are normal. Look for her baptism or birth registration to settle it, and keep noting the variations.

head: Country
What survives
rows: 1841–1921, every ten years. Names everyone from 1841; relationships from 1851. 1931 was destroyed in 1942; there was no 1941 census, but the 1939 Register fills the gap.
1901 and 1911 survive almost complete. Most of the 1800s is lost; see Griffith's Valuation instead.
Every ten years from 1790. Names everyone from 1850; relationships from 1880. Most of 1890 burned in 1921. Released after 72 years, so 1950 is the latest.

blocks.p: Always read the pages before and after your family. Relatives often lived on the same street, and the neighbours may be the in-laws you haven't found yet.

takeaways: Every column is a separate clue with its own reliability.
Ages and birthplaces drift. Look for consistency across several censuses.
Read the neighbours: families clustered.

lessons.title: Parish registers and old dates
lessons.dek: Before the state kept records, the church did. Learn their language, their gaps, and the calendar they used.

blocks.p: Church registers are the deepest well in family history. In England some go back to 1538; in much of Catholic Europe to the late 1500s. They're also where research gets harder: entries are shorter, often in Latin, and written in hands you'll need practice to read.

list: **Baptisms** give the child's name, the baptism date, and usually the father. Later registers add the mother, an address and the father's trade. Catholic and Lutheran registers often name godparents too.
**Marriages** give the couple, the date, and sometimes their parishes and witnesses. Before civil registration, they rarely name parents.
**Banns** were read on three Sundays before a wedding, in the parishes of both bride and groom. A banns entry can tell you where the other partner came from.
**Burials** may give only a name and date. The age and residence, when given, help tell people with the same name apart.

blocks.p: Catholic registers across Europe, and some early Anglican ones, were kept in Latin. You don't need to learn the language, just about forty words. Tap a card to turn it over.

blocks.h: When the year started in March

blocks.p: Until 1752, England and its colonies started the legal year on 25 March, not 1 January. A baby born in February 1731 would be born in what we'd call February 1732. Careful writers used double dates: **10 February 1731/2**.

In 1752 Britain also switched from the Julian to the Gregorian calendar, and 2 September was followed by 14 September. Catholic countries switched much earlier, mostly from 1582. If a date seems to be eleven days off, this is usually why.

quiz.q: A register says a child was baptised on 3 March 1720, and its parents married on 20 May 1720. Is something wrong?
o: Yes: the child was born before the marriage
Not necessarily: 3 March 1720 came after 20 May 1720 in the old calendar
Yes: one of the dates must be a transcription error
quiz.why: Under the old style, 1720 began on 25 March, so March 1–24 were the last days of the year. 3 March 1720 is 3 March 1721 in modern terms, about nine months after the wedding.

blocks.p: In England, parishes sent a yearly copy of their register to the bishop. When a register is damaged or missing, these copies can fill the gap, and they sometimes differ from the original in useful ways.

takeaways: Baptism isn't birth, and marriage records before civil registration rarely name parents.
About forty Latin words will carry you through most Catholic registers.
Before 1752 in Britain, January to March dates belong to the previous year.

lessons.title: Following migrants
lessons.dek: To cross an ocean in your research, you need the name of a town, not a country. Work backwards to find it.

blocks.p: Finding that an ancestor came “from Hungary” or “from Ireland” is not enough to cross the ocean. Records abroad are kept by parish, district or town. The single most important goal in immigrant research is the name of the **place of origin**, and you almost always find it in records created *after* they arrived.

blocks.h: Work backwards from the new country

order.prompt: Put these searches in the order you'd usually do them, starting with the most recent. Tap them in turn.
items: Death record and obituary in the new country
Census entries showing year of immigration
Naturalization papers, which may name the town and ship
Passenger list for the arrival
Church or civil records in the town of origin
order.why: Later records are easier to find and often state the earlier facts you need. Naturalization papers after 1906 in the US usually give the exact town and ship, which leads to the passenger list, which leads home.

blocks.p: US arrival lists exist from 1820, and from the 1890s they ask far more: last residence, the nearest relative left behind, and who the passenger was joining. Departure lists survive from some ports too. Hamburg's, from 1850 to 1934, are a major source for Central and Eastern Europeans. Most of Bremen's were destroyed.

blocks.t: Names weren't changed at Ellis Island
blocks.p: Passenger lists were drawn up by the shipping company at the port of departure, and inspectors checked passengers against them. Names were changed later, usually by the immigrants themselves or their children, often at naturalization. Search for the original spelling.

Borders have shifted many times. A town recorded as being in Hungary in 1900 may be in Slovakia, Romania or Serbia today, under a different name. Gazetteers, place dictionaries from the time, tell you which parish and civil district a village belonged to.

quiz.q: József Varga's 1938 death certificate in Ohio says he was born in “Hungary.” What's your best next step?
o: Search Hungarian church records for every József Varga born around 1870
Look for his US naturalization papers and his arrival record
Assume he was from Budapest
quiz.why: Varga is one of the most common Hungarian surnames. Without a town, searching Hungary is hopeless. Naturalization and passenger records are where the town usually appears.

takeaways: Your goal is the town of origin. Look for it in the new country first.
Work backwards: death, census, naturalization, passenger list, then home.
Check old gazetteers: borders and place names change.

lessons.title: Wills, land and the courts
lessons.dek: Property left paper trails. Wills and deeds often state relationships outright, which no census does.

blocks.p: If an ancestor owned anything, even a little, it may have left a record when it changed hands. Wills, probate inventories, deeds and court cases are among the few records that state family relationships in so many words, often generations before civil registration.
Wills follow a formula, so the interesting part is what changes: who's named, how they're described, and who's left out. Tap the highlighted phrases in this invented will.

clues.title: Will of Samuel Pell of Wigan, yeoman (example)
clues.text: In the name of God Amen. I [[Samuel Pell of Wigan in the County of Lancaster, yeoman|A place and status. ‘Yeoman’ means a farmer who owned or held land on a long lease: look for deeds and tax records.]], being weak in body but of sound mind, do make this my last will. I give unto [[my loving wife Martha|Martha was alive when the will was written. Compare the will date and probate date to bracket Samuel's death.]] the use of my dwelling house for the term of her natural life. I give unto [[my son William|A son named outright. This is direct evidence of the relationship.]] my loom and all my tools. I give unto [[my daughter Sarah, now the wife of Peter Lowe|Sarah's married name and her husband, in one phrase. Search for the Lowe–Pell marriage.]] the sum of five pounds. I give unto [[my grandson Samuel, son of my late son John|John died before his father, and had a son named after his grandfather. A whole branch you may not have known about.]] the sum of two pounds. I appoint [[my trusty friend Thomas Crook|Executors and witnesses are often relatives or close neighbours. Ann Crook married William Pell in 1868: is Thomas her father?]] sole executor.

blocks.p: Relationship words have shifted. **Son-in-law** could mean a stepson. **Cousin** could mean a niece, nephew or almost any relative. **Junior** and **Senior** could just mean the younger and older of two men with the same name in town, not father and son. **Now wife** can hint that there was an earlier one.

Deeds record who sold land to whom, and when heirs sold inherited land they often all signed together, naming spouses. In the US, early federal land sales are searchable at the Bureau of Land Management, and county deed books are mostly on FamilySearch. FamilySearch's full-text search now lets you search the handwriting of millions of deeds and wills by name.

Court records capture families at their most dramatic: debts, disputes over inheritances, guardianships of orphans, crimes. A guardianship case can name all the children of a man who died young. Criminal records, like those of the Old Bailey in London, can describe an ancestor's appearance and words in astonishing detail.

quiz.q: A will was written in March 1879 and proved in court in January 1880. What does that tell you about the testator's death?
o: He died in March 1879
He died between March 1879 and January 1880
He died in January 1880
quiz.why: He was alive when he signed the will, and dead by the time it was proved. That brackets the death, so you know which burial registers to search.

takeaways: Wills and deeds often state relationships outright.
Read the formula for what changes: who's named, who's left out, and how.
Old relationship words don't always mean what they mean today.

lessons.title: Sources, information and evidence
lessons.dek: Not all records are equal. Professionals judge each one in three ways before deciding what it proves.

blocks.p: Beginners ask “Is this record right?” Experienced researchers ask three smaller questions instead: what kind of **source** is it, where did its **information** come from, and what **evidence** does it give for the question I'm asking? This vocabulary comes from Elizabeth Shown Mills and the Board for Certification of Genealogists, and it's used across the field.

An **original** source is the first recording of an event, like the register a vicar wrote in. A **derivative** is copied, transcribed, indexed or abstracted from something else, like a website index or a typed transcript. Each copy is a chance for error. An **authored work**, like a published family history, is someone's conclusions drawn from many sources.

Information is judged piece by piece. **Primary** information comes from someone who witnessed the event: a mother giving her baby's birth date. **Secondary** information is secondhand: a son giving his late father's birthplace on a death certificate. One record usually holds both.

blocks.h: 3. The evidence: direct, indirect or negative?

blocks.p: Evidence only exists in relation to a question. **Direct** evidence answers it on its own: “William, son of Samuel Pell.” **Indirect** evidence has to be combined with other facts to answer it, like an age that points to a birth year. **Negative** evidence is the meaningful absence of something you'd expect to find, like a man missing from a tax list the year after he's said to have died.

sort.prompt: For a death certificate from 1938, classify each piece of information.
items: The date of death, given by the attending doctor
Primary: the doctor was present at or near the time.
The deceased's birthplace, given by his son
Secondary: the son wasn't there when his father was born.
The cause of death
Primary: the doctor's own observation.
The names of the deceased's parents
Secondary: the informant is reporting what he was told, often decades earlier.
The place of burial, given by the undertaker
Primary: the undertaker arranged it.

blocks.t: Why a death certificate gets birth dates wrong
blocks.p: A death certificate is an excellent source for the death and a weak one for the birth. The informant was grieving, often guessing, and had never seen the birth. Look for a record made at the time instead.

quiz.q: An online index says Edith Ashworth was born on 12 May 1897. What kind of source is the index?
o: Original
Derivative
Authored work
quiz.why: An index is derived from another record. Find the image of the original register or certificate it was made from.

takeaways: Ask three questions: what source, whose information, what evidence.
Prefer originals over copies, and primary information over secondhand.
Evidence only exists relative to a question.

lessons.title: Cite as you go
lessons.dek: A citation is a note to your future self: where this came from, and how to find it again.

blocks.p: Six months from now you won't remember which census told you Hannah was born in Bury, or whether you saw the image or just an index. A citation answers that in a line. It also lets anyone else check your work, which is what makes a family history trustworthy.
Formats vary, and *Evidence Explained* by Elizabeth Shown Mills is the standard guide for genealogy. But almost every good citation answers the same five questions:

list: **Who** created the record? (Name the person or office.)
**What** is it? (The title or a description.)
**When** was it made? (And when the event happened, if different.)
**Where in** the source is the item? (Page, entry, folio, image number.)
**Where is** the source? (The archive, or the website and collection, with the date you looked.)

blocks.p: If you saw an index on a website, cite the index on that website, not the original register it was made from. If you later view the register, cite that too. Your citation should never claim more than you looked at.

quiz.q: You found a baptism in a FreeREG transcription. Which is the honest citation?
o: The parish register of St Peter, Bolton, entry for 4 May 1814
FreeREG transcription of the St Peter, Bolton baptisms, entry for 4 May 1814, viewed 26 October 2026
FreeREG
quiz.why: You saw a transcription, so cite the transcription, with enough detail to find the entry again. Then order or view the original register and cite that separately.

takeaways: Cite every fact the moment you record it.
Answer who, what, when, where in, and where is.
Cite what you actually saw, not the original behind it.

lessons.title: When records disagree
lessons.dek: Conflicting records are not a dead end. Weighing them carefully is how real conclusions are made.

blocks.p: Sooner or later two records will disagree. A birth year differs by four years, a surname appears two ways, a birthplace changes county. Beginners pick the one they like. Researchers line everything up and weigh it.

blocks.h: A real problem from the example tree

blocks.p: In the example family, Ann, wife of William Pell, appears as **Ann Crook** on her marriage and **Ann Cook** on one child's birth certificate. Which is right? Gather every record, and judge each one.

head: Record
Name given
Who gave it
Weight
rows: Moderate: original, but given by her husband
Ann, daughter of Thomas and Jane Crook
Strong, if it's the same Ann

blocks.p: The marriage is an original record with primary information, and she signed it. The birth certificate was given by her husband and could easily have misheard “Crook” or been miswritten by the registrar. A baptism for an Ann Crook with a father named Thomas fits too, and Thomas Crook appears as executor of the Pell will in Lesson 8. The weight of evidence points to **Crook**.
Whatever you decide, record why in the person's notes: which records conflict, which you trust more, and why. A future researcher, maybe you, will have the same doubt.

One of the best tools for finding errors is a simple timeline. Put every event for a person in order with their age at each. Problems leap out: a mother aged 9 at a birth, a child born after a father's burial, a man in two places on census night.

quiz.q: A tree shows Hannah Kay, born 1814, as the mother of a child born in 1866. What's the most likely explanation?
o: Late motherhood: it happens
The child probably belongs to a different Hannah, or a daughter of Hannah
Her birth year is certainly wrong
quiz.why: She'd have been 52. Not quite impossible, but very rare. Far more likely is a merged identity, or a grandchild entered as a child. Check the baptism or birth record of the child for the mother's name.

quiz.q: Which conflict should usually be resolved in favour of the earlier record?
o: An age at marriage versus an age at death
A middle name given at baptism versus one given in a newspaper notice 70 years later
Both of these
quiz.why: Records made closer to the event, by people closer to it, tend to be more reliable. This is a rule of thumb, not a law: an earlier derivative copy can still be worse than a later original.

takeaways: Gather every record before deciding anything.
Weigh each one: original or copy, firsthand or secondhand, made when and by whom.
Write your reasoning down, and use timelines to catch impossible people.

lessons.title: Plans and logs
lessons.dek: Researchers who plan find more in less time, and never search the same register twice.

blocks.p: It's easy to spend an evening clicking from site to site, finding interesting things and remembering none of them. A research plan turns that into a focused search, and a research log means you never repeat it.

list: **Objective.** One specific question: “Who were the parents of Ann Crook, who married William Pell in Wigan in 1868?” Not “find out about the Crooks.”
**Known facts.** Everything you've proven so far, with sources.
**Working hypothesis.** Your best guess, stated so it can be tested: “Ann was the daughter of Thomas and Jane Crook of Wigan.”
**Sources to search.** A list of the specific records that could confirm or disprove it, best first.
**Results.** What each search found, including what it didn't.

blocks.p: A research log lists every search: the date, the source, what you searched for, and the result. “Searched Wigan baptisms 1844–1852 for Ann Crook: none found” is valuable. It stops you searching again, and the absence itself can become evidence.

blocks.h: Make a plan for someone in your tree

blocks.p: Pick a person and this builds a starting plan from what's already in your tree. Add it to their notes, then refine it.

blocks.t: Plan for one question at a time
blocks.p: The narrower the objective, the better the plan. Once it's answered, write a new one. Professionals often run several small plans for one ancestor, one after another.

takeaways: Ask one specific question at a time.
State a hypothesis you can test, and list sources to test it.
Log every search, including those that found nothing.

lessons.title: The FAN club
lessons.dek: When one person's records run out, research the people around them. Their records often hold the answer.

blocks.p: People didn't live alone. They moved with neighbours, married friends' sisters, chose relatives as godparents and asked cousins to witness their wills. Elizabeth Shown Mills named this the **FAN club**: Friends, Associates and Neighbours. When your ancestor's own records go silent, theirs may not.

list: **Witnesses** at weddings and on wills and deeds
**Godparents** and sponsors at baptisms
**Neighbours** on the census page and tax lists
**Executors, sureties and bondsmen**
People who **migrated together**, or arrived on the same ship
Members of the same church, lodge or regiment

blocks.p: Tap the names in this invented marriage entry that you'd add to your cluster research.

clues.title: Marriage, St Catharine's, Wigan, 1868 (example)
clues.text: No. 214. [[William Pell|The groom, the person you're researching.]], 23, bachelor, weaver, of [[Scholes|A district of Wigan. Note it for the census and directories.]], father [[Samuel Pell, weaver|Matches the will in Lesson 8.]]. Ann Crook, 20, spinster, of [[Scholes|Same district as the groom. Neighbours marrying neighbours: search the 1861 census of Scholes for both families.]], father [[Thomas Crook, collier|Her father's name and trade. Look for his death, his will, and a Thomas Crook in Wigan baptisms around 1820.]]. Married after banns. Witnesses: [[Peter Lowe|Peter Lowe married William's sister Sarah: a family witness.]] and [[Jane Crook|Possibly Ann's mother or sister. Witnesses were very often relatives.]].

blocks.p: Make a list of names that appear repeatedly around your ancestor. Then research each of them with the same care as a direct ancestor: where did *they* come from? If six families arrive in a town in the same year from the same place, and you can find where five came from, the sixth very likely came from there too.

quiz.q: Your ancestor appears from nowhere in an 1830s tax list. Which is the most promising next step?
o: Search the whole country for men of the same name
Note the names listed next to him and trace where those neighbours came from
Wait for a DNA match
quiz.why: Tax lists were often compiled in the order the assessor walked. Neighbours who arrived at the same time often came from the same place.

takeaways: Research the people around your ancestor, not just your ancestor.
Witnesses, godparents and neighbours were often relatives.
Migrations happened in groups: trace the group.

lessons.title: Brick walls and hidden records
lessons.dek: Most brick walls are not missing records. They're records nobody has looked in yet, or assumptions nobody has checked.

blocks.p: A “brick wall” is the point where an ancestor's trail seems to stop. They feel permanent, but most fall to one of two things: searching records that aren't indexed online, or questioning something you assumed early on.
Go back over what you think you know, and ask where each fact came from. Tick each statement you can back with an original record.

items: I know their name from a record made during their life, not a descendant's memory
Their age comes from more than one record
I've confirmed the place name, and which parish or county it belonged to at the time
I've checked whether county or parish boundaries changed
I've searched for every spelling variant and nickname
I've looked for siblings, not just the direct ancestor
I've looked at the original images, not only the index
I've researched their witnesses, neighbours and godparents

blocks.p: Huge numbers of records are online as images only. The **FamilySearch Catalog** is the way in: search it by place, not by name, and work through every heading for the town and county. Tax records, court minutes, poor law papers and land books are listed there and searched almost by no one.

list: **ArchiveGrid**, **Archives Hub** and The National Archives' **Discovery** list collections held in local archives that have never been filmed.
**FamilySearch Full-Text Search** reads handwriting with AI. It finds names inside deeds and wills that were never indexed.
**Local histories and newspapers** mention people who appear in no official record.

blocks.p: In the US especially, counties split and new ones formed constantly. A family that never moved may appear in three counties' records over 40 years. Check the county's formation date before deciding records don't exist.

Women are the most common brick walls, because they change surnames and appear less in property and court records. Work through their children's records (a birth certificate gives the mother's maiden name), their husband's will, their own death, and the witnesses at their marriage.

quiz.q: You've searched every index for a family's baptisms in a parish and found nothing. What should you check next?
o: Whether the register's images exist in the FamilySearch Catalog under that parish
Whether the family moved to another country
Nothing: the baptisms weren't recorded
quiz.why: Indexes cover only some registers, and some years. The images may be there to browse, page by page.

takeaways: Audit your assumptions before searching further.
Search catalogs by place to find unindexed records.
Check boundaries, and follow women through their children and husbands.

lessons.title: Old handwriting and languages
lessons.dek: Old documents aren't unreadable, just unfamiliar. Learn a dozen letterforms and you can read most of them.

blocks.p: The first time you open a register from the 1700s it can look like a foreign script. It isn't. Writers used a handful of letter shapes and abbreviations we've since dropped. Learn those, and read slowly, and most pages open up.
Until about 1800, a lower-case s at the start or in the middle of a word was usually written **ſ**, the long s. It looks like an f without the full crossbar. A double s was often written ſs or ſſ.

o: Blefsed are the meek
Blessed are the meek
Bleffed are the meek
quiz.why: The first s is a long s, the second a short one. Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century printers used the same convention.

o: Elizabeth Haslam, spinster
Elizabeth Haflam, fpinfter
Elizabeth Hallam, spinster
quiz.why: Three long s's. Once you see them, you can't miss them.

blocks.h: Other letters that trip people up

list: **u and v** were interchangeable: ‘vnto’ is ‘unto’, ‘haue’ is ‘have’.
**i and j** were interchangeable: ‘Iohn’ is ‘John’.
**ff** at the start of a name is a capital F: ‘ffrancis’ is ‘Francis’.
**y** often stood for an old letter, thorn, meaning ‘th’: ‘ye’ is ‘the’, ‘yt’ is ‘that’.
Abbreviations were marked with a line above or a raised letter: ‘wm’ is William, ‘Jno’ is John, ‘Chas’ is Charles.

blocks.t: Build an alphabet from the page
blocks.p: When you can't read a word, find letters you're sure of elsewhere on the same page: in the names you know, the place name, the year. Copy each letterform out. The same hand writes every letter the same way.

If your family came from Germany, look up the **Kurrent** script before anything else: German records were written in it until the 1940s, and several letters look nothing like their modern forms. FamilySearch publishes word lists for dozens of languages with just the vocabulary genealogists need.

takeaways: Learn the long s, u/v, i/j, ff and y for th.
Build an alphabet from the same hand on the same page.
Word lists for each language cover the few hundred words you need.

lessons.title: DNA as evidence
lessons.dek: A DNA test doesn't hand you a family tree. It gives you evidence, and like any evidence it has to be weighed with records.

blocks.p: DNA testing has opened walls that records never could: unknown fathers, adoptions, families separated by slavery or war. But a list of matches isn't a tree. DNA tells you *that* you're related to someone and roughly *how closely*. Records tell you *how*.

head: Test
Follows
Best for
rows: All your lines, roughly back five or six generations
Finding cousins on every side; the test most companies sell
Father to son only, the direct paternal line
Surname studies and one paternal line, very far back. Only men carry it.
Mother to child, the direct maternal line
One maternal line, very far back, usually too far for records

quiz.q: You want to know whether two Ashworth men in different countries descend from the same Ashworth father in the 1700s. Which test fits best?
o: Autosomal
Y-DNA
mtDNA
quiz.why: Y-DNA passes almost unchanged from father to son, as surnames usually do. Comparing two direct-line male Ashworths can show a shared paternal ancestor many generations back.

blocks.p: Testing companies tell you how much DNA you share with a match, measured in **centimorgans** (cM). More shared DNA means a closer relationship, but every relationship has a wide range, and the ranges overlap. Try a number from a real match.

list: **Start with matches who have trees**, and look for surnames and places you recognise.
**Group your matches.** The Leeds Method sorts your closer cousin matches into clusters, which usually line up with your four grandparents.
**Use shared matches.** If two matches share DNA with you and with each other, they probably connect through the same line.
**Build trees for matches who haven't.** It's slow, and it's how most unknown-parentage cases are solved.

blocks.p: DNA can reveal unknown siblings, adoptions and different biological fathers, for you or for others. Think about what you'll do if that happens before you test, and handle what you find about living people with great care.

takeaways: DNA shows that you're related, and roughly how closely. Records show how.
Choose the test for the question: autosomal, Y-DNA or mtDNA.
Shared cM ranges overlap. Use them with trees and records, never alone.

lessons.title: Proving it, and passing it on
lessons.dek: The final skill: a conclusion others can trust, written down so it outlives you.

blocks.p: Everything in this course leads here. A conclusion is only as good as the reasoning behind it, and only useful if someone else can follow it. Professional genealogists measure their conclusions against one standard.
The Board for Certification of Genealogists sets out five elements. A conclusion that meets all five can be called proved, though new evidence can always reopen it.

order.prompt: Put the five elements in their usual order. Tap them in turn.
items: Reasonably exhaustive research
Complete and accurate source citations
Thorough analysis and correlation of the evidence
Resolution of any conflicting evidence
A soundly reasoned, coherently written conclusion
order.why: Search widely, cite everything, analyse and correlate it, resolve the conflicts, then write it down. Each element depends on the ones before.

blocks.p: Not every fact needs an essay. When records state something plainly and agree, a citation is enough. When you've combined indirect evidence or resolved a conflict, write a short **proof summary**: what the question was, which records you used, how they fit together, and why the conflicts don't change the answer. The notes field on each person in this app is a good place for it.

Names and dates are the skeleton. Social history is the flesh: what a cotton spinner's day was like in 1870s Bolton, what a crossing from Hamburg cost, what the 1918 flu did to a town. Put your ancestors' lives in their world, and the people you've found will make sense to the family who read about them.

blocks.h: Protect the living, preserve the dead

list: Don't publish details of living people without their permission.
Keep copies of your research in more than one place, in formats that will still open in thirty years.
Scan photographs and documents at high resolution, and write down who and what they show.
Share with relatives, and with archives and societies who'll keep it after you.

quiz.q: You've concluded that Ann Crook was the daughter of Thomas Crook, using a baptism, a marriage, a will and a census. What's left to do to meet the standard?
o: Nothing: four records are enough
Check you've searched every reasonable source, cite each record, and write down how they fit together and why the ‘Cook’ spelling doesn't change the answer
Find a fifth record
quiz.why: The standard isn't a number of records. It's whether your search was reasonably exhaustive, your sources are cited, and your reasoning is written down where someone else can follow it.

takeaways: Measure conclusions against the five elements of the Genealogical Proof Standard.
Write a proof summary whenever you combine evidence or resolve a conflict.
Put ancestors in their world, protect the living, and preserve your work.
